sections.heading: Ryan W. Bavis > About
sections.text: Humans and other animals typically respond to acute changes in oxygen or carbon dioxide concentrations with protective changes in breathing, metabolic rate, and/or body temperature. How and why do these responses differ within and across species? How much of this variation is a product of an individual’s developmental age or a product of their environment (i.e., plasticity)? When is this variation beneficial and when is it maladaptive? These are the types of questions that are regularly addressed by students working in my lab. Students usually test their hypotheses on rats, quail, or anoles, although we’ve worked with a variety of other vertebrate and invertebrate animal models. Techniques commonly used in the lab include noninvasive measurements of breathing and metabolism, in vitro electrophysiological recordings of carotid body chemoreceptor activity, and a variety of histological and molecular assays. Please contact me if you want to learn more about research opportunities in my lab.

sections.heading: Dylan J. Freas > About
sections.text: Organic chemistry permeates our daily lives– from the aroma of a cup of coffee to the fuel in our cars and the fibers in our clothing, organic compounds play a important role. Within biomedical science, synthetic organic compounds have revolutionized healthcare as targeted drugs and advanced biomaterials. As we strive to develop more precise and effective medications, which sometimes have increasingly sophisticated chemical structures, it’s important for us to discover new fundamental methods to break and form chemical bonds. My research focuses on developing new chemical reactions of organic compounds and applying them to the synthesis of biologically useful small molecules and degradable polymers. Students in my lab will gain experience in many aspects of organic synthesis, including designing multistep syntheses, optimizing chemical reactions, and using chromatography and spectroscopy to characterize small molecules and polymers. We will also (eventually!) test the biocompatibility and biological activity of the products we make!

sections.heading: Geneva Laurita > About
sections.text: Research: My research interests focus on understanding the structure—property relationships of inorganic solid state materials, particularly those of relevance to energy and electronics-related technology. Through understanding the arrangement of the atoms in a material, we can explain how atomic interactions give rise to various physical properties, such as how a material interacts with light or conducts electricity. I am particularly interested in utilizing advanced neutron and synchrotron X-ray scattering techniques to gain a detailed understanding of the structure of a material. Research in my laboratory focuses on solid state synthesis and characterization techniques with an emphasis on scattering experiments performed at national laboratories.

sections.heading: Susan A. Dewsnap > About
sections.text: Susan exhibits her ceramic work nationally and internationally with awards from the National Council on Education for the Ceramic Arts Biennial, the World Ceramic Biennale Korea International Competition, and Best of Show in the Strictly Functional Pottery National Exhibition. Her ceramic study began at a community clay studio in Boulder, Colorado and matured through intensive summer workshops at Haystack Mountain School in Maine and The Penland School in North Carolina. Susan received a BFA in painting from the University of New Hampshire and a MFA in ceramics from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, where she also taught from 2008 through 2012.  Her work is represented in galleries across the United States.

sections.heading: Trian Nguyen > About
sections.text: Dr. Trian Nguyen is Associate Professor of Art and Visual Culture and a core faculty member in the Asian Studies Program at Bates College, where he joined in 2000 as the college’s first specialist in Asian art history. He teaches a wide array of courses on Asian visual culture, regularly leads students abroad to experience artistic traditions firsthand. His research explores Buddhist art and architecture in Southeast Asia, with a dedicated specialization in Vietnamese visual culture. More recently, his fieldwork has centered on the Daoist ritual art of the Yao ethnic minority across southern China and Southeast Asia, examining their spiritual traditions through ceremonial scrolls, ritual objects, and historical manuscripts. His scholarship—published internationally in both English and Vietnamese—is driven by a passion for sharing these rich, often understudied cultural heritage traditions with broader global audiences. With an interdisciplinary academic background, Dr. Nguyen holds a Ph.D. in Asian Art History from UC Berkeley, a Master of Theological Studies from Harvard Divinity School, and a B.A. in Eastern Philosophy and Chinese Studies from San Francisco State University. His contributions to the field have been recognized through prestigious honors, including two Fulbright research grants in Vietnam and a residency fellowship at the Center for Advanced Study in the Visual Arts (CASVA) at the National Gallery of Art. Outside the classroom and field research, he finds immense joy in mentoring students, fostering cross-cultural understanding, and bringing living artistic traditions into everyday learning.

sections.heading: Patrick W. Otim > About
sections.text: My second book project, supported by a fellowship from the National Endowment for the Humanities and a Philips Fellowship, is tentatively titled Caught in between the Warring Parties: A History of Terror and Survival in Northern Uganda, 1950–2008 . This project aims to offer a fresh look at the war between the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA) and the government of Uganda (GoU). Specifically, it seeks to shift the focus away from the LRA, the GoU, and the different categories of victims—such as child soldiers, women who were abducted and forced to marry LRA commanders and bear their children, and victims of wartime sexual crimes—to everyday, ordinary people who experienced the war in their homes or camps. At its core, the project asks: How did ordinary civilians manage to keep alive? I am hoping not only to uncover decisions and choices ordinary people made during wartime, but also to offer a more nuanced insight into the multiple contours of sufferings of everyday ordinary people.

sections.heading: Anderson Moss-Weaver > About
sections.text: Anderson C. Moss-Weaver is an Assistant Professor of religious studies whose interdisciplinary approach traces alternative religious worldbuilding in 20th-century African American literature. His research highlights how Black authors have used literature to produce symbols, rituals, myths, and new conceptions of the divine. He examines how Black literary artists have used literature to answer questions of ultimate existential meaning, especially as they have sought to formulate sacred aesthetics of freedom that transcend freedom’s normative Western political conception. He also has secondary research interests in the history of Afro-Asian solidarities. In his classes, he regularly incorporates ways that Black and Asian people have worked together to form collective identities and resist racism in America. He teaches courses on theories and methods of interpreting religion, the histories of African American religions, metaphysical religions in America, and the intersections of religion and the arts.
